entities.summary:
Plato (c. 428–348 BCE) was an Athenian philosopher whose dialogues, Academy, and Theory of Forms established the foundation of Western philosophy, metaphysics, and political theory. Born to Athenian aristocracy, he became Socrates's most brilliant student.

Socrates's execution in 399 BCE transformed Plato's life. After traveling to Egypt, Italy, and Syracuse, he founded the Academy (c. 387 BCE) — the Western world's first institution of higher learning, which operated for over 900 years.

His 36 dialogues explored justice (Republic), love (Symposium), the soul's immortality (Phaedo), and reality's nature (Timaeus). The Theory of Forms posited that the physical world is a shadow of eternal, perfect Ideas — most famously illustrated in the Allegory of the Cave.

Alfred North Whitehead declared that 'the European philosophical tradition consists of a series of footnotes to Plato.' His influence permeates Christian theology, Islamic philosophy, Renaissance humanism, and modern political theory.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Plato's Academy, founded in 387 BCE, was the first institution of higher learning in the Western world, shaping Western philosophy and education for over 900 years. His Theory of Forms had a profound impact on metaphysics and political theory.
